items.followUp: Define unicellular and multicellular organization, giving one example of each.

rubric.description: Defines cellular organization as the arrangement of cells in an organism.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition linking cells and their arrangement in an organism.

rubric.description: States that a single cell performs all life functions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the one-cell organization and its function.

rubric.description: States that similar cells live together in a colony.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing cells grouped as a colony.

rubric.why: Explains multicellular organization and its specialization.
rubric.description: States that many cells form the organism and are specialized for different functions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for many cells and 1 mark for specialization or division of labour.

modelAnswer: Cellular organization is the arrangement of cells in an organism.
In unicellular organization, a single cell performs all the life functions, as in Amoeba.
In colonial organization, similar cells live together in a colony, as in Volvox.
In multicellular organization, many specialized cells work together, with a division of labour, as in plants and animals.

items.followUp: Name and briefly describe the functions of four types of epithelial tissue.

rubric.description: Squamous cells are thin and flat, supporting diffusion or lining surfaces.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the name and a correct feature or function.

rubric.description: Cuboidal cells are cube-shaped and commonly perform secretion or absorption.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the name and a correct feature or function.

rubric.description: Column-shaped cells commonly perform absorption or secretion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the name and a correct feature or function.

rubric.why: Recognizes another epithelial type and its function.
rubric.description: Describes ciliated, glandular or stratified epithelium with a suitable function.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming one of these types and giving its correct function.

modelAnswer: Epithelial tissues cover body surfaces, line internal organs and cavities, and form glands.
Squamous epithelium consists of thin, flat cells; it forms a lining and allows diffusion.
Cuboidal epithelium consists of cube-shaped cells and is involved in secretion and absorption.
Columnar epithelium consists of tall cells and commonly performs absorption and secretion.
Ciliated epithelium has cilia that move materials such as mucus; glandular epithelium is specialized for secretion.

items.followUp: Describe how temperature and pH affect enzyme action, including what happens at their optimum values.

rubric.why: Explains the effect of rising temperature below the optimum.
rubric.description: States that enzyme action generally increases as temperature rises towards the optimum.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the increase in rate up to the optimum.

rubric.why: Explains the optimum temperature and the effect of excessive heat.
rubric.description: Identifies the optimum temperature as the point of maximum activity and explains that higher temperatures denature the enzyme or alter its active site.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for maximum activity at the optimum and 1 mark for denaturation or active-site change above it.

rubric.why: Explains that enzymes have an optimum pH.
rubric.description: States that each enzyme works best at a particular pH.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the enzyme's optimum pH.

rubric.why: Explains the effect of pH away from the optimum.
rubric.description: States that pH changes away from the optimum alter the active site or reduce enzyme activity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct effect of unsuitable pH.

modelAnswer: As temperature rises, enzyme activity increases because molecules move faster and collide more often, up to the optimum temperature.
At the optimum temperature, the enzyme works at its maximum rate.
Above the optimum, heat changes the enzyme's shape and active site; the enzyme is denatured and its activity falls.
Each enzyme has a particular optimum pH at which it works fastest.
A pH above or below the optimum changes the active site or denatures the enzyme, so the reaction rate decreases.

items.followUp: Explain how ATP releases energy for cellular activities and how it is replenished.

rubric.why: Identifies ATP as the cell's energy currency.
rubric.description: States that ATP is the chief energy currency or immediate energy carrier of cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying ATP's role as an energy carrier.

rubric.description: States that energy is associated with ATP's phosphate bonds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for connecting stored energy with a phosphate bond.

rubric.description: States that ATP breakdown or hydrolysis forms ADP and phosphate and releases energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the breakdown products or release of energy.

rubric.description: States that released energy powers cell activities and ATP is regenerated using energy from respiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing its use in cell work or its regeneration.

modelAnswer: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the chief energy currency of cells because it transfers usable energy to cellular activities.
Energy is stored in the bonds between ATP's phosphate groups.
When ATP is hydrolysed, it forms ADP and phosphate and releases energy.
Cells use this energy for activities such as synthesis, movement and active transport; energy from respiration is used to regenerate ATP from ADP and phosphate.

items.followUp: Name two macronutrients and two micronutrients required by plants, and state one function of nitrogen.

rubric.description: States that macronutrients are nutrients required by plants in large quantities.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the large-quantity requirement.

rubric.description: States that micronutrients are nutrients required by plants in small quantities.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the small-quantity requirement.

rubric.why: Gives a major role of nitrogen.
rubric.description: States that nitrogen is needed to make amino acids or proteins.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct nitrogen-containing product.

rubric.description: States that nitrogen is a component of nucleic acids such as DNA or RNA.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying nucleic acids.

rubric.why: Gives a further role or effect of nitrogen.
rubric.description: States that nitrogen is needed for chlorophyll or normal growth, or describes yellowing due to deficiency.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct additional role or deficiency effect.

modelAnswer: Macronutrients are nutrients required by plants in large quantities.
Micronutrients are nutrients required by plants in small quantities.
Nitrogen is needed to make amino acids and proteins.
It is also a component of nucleic acids such as DNA and RNA.
Nitrogen supports chlorophyll formation and normal plant growth; its deficiency can cause yellowing and poor growth.

items.followUp: Define transpiration and explain how humidity, wind and light affect its rate.

rubric.description: Defines transpiration as loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through stomata.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for water-vapour loss from plant parts or stomata.

rubric.why: Describes the effect of light or temperature.
rubric.description: States that greater light or temperature generally increases transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correctly described direction of effect.

rubric.description: States that high humidity lowers transpiration, while dry air increases it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct humidity relationship.

rubric.why: Describes the effect of wind or water availability.
rubric.description: States that wind usually increases transpiration or that water shortage reduces it through stomatal closure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct factor and its effect.

modelAnswer: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata.
Increased light and temperature generally increase the rate of transpiration.
High humidity decreases transpiration, whereas dry air increases it.
Wind or moving air generally increases transpiration by carrying away moist air around the leaf.
A shortage of soil water may cause stomata to close, reducing transpiration.

Kitab al-Ibil (Book of Camels).
